section_summary: This section completes one weekly press survey and contains four further despatches analyzing Japanese newspaper reactions to elections, labor policy, economic stabilization, foreign investment, Asian security, and international affairs in January and early February 1949. It also includes a short internal summary and a transmittal despatch enclosing The Japanese Press, Past and Present, 1949. The enclosure begins with maps, front matter, contents, advertisements, an account of the Japan Newspaper Publishers' and Editors' Association, its Canons of Journalism, and the opening of a history of the Japanese press.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 10: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending January 6, 1949
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch surveys Japanese press reactions to New Year developments, elections, China, agriculture, forced labor and the Allied Council for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The concluding pages quote optimistic newspaper assessments of Japan's stabilization during 1948 and discuss reactions to General MacArthur's New Year's message and the restored use of the Japanese flag. Editorials address election candidates and parties, the Chinese Civil War and Chiang Kai-shek's peace proposal, and the relationship between developments in China and Japan's international position. The despatch also reviews agricultural reform, crop-delivery burdens, a report about forced-labor brokers in northern Honshu, and coverage of the Allied Council's discussion of Japanese policing.

subfiles.title: Internal Summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 22
subfiles.from: Department of State staff; routing initials partly illegible
subfiles.about: The memorandum condenses the principal findings of Tokyo Despatch No. 22 concerning Japanese press reactions for the week ending January 13.
subfiles.summary: The summary notes press support for labor-law revision, criticism of police selection and training, and exhortations for greater electoral participation. It records the Nippon Times's attack on the electoral law, the denial by GHQ of plans for a purge-appeal committee, and widespread concern over rice prices and farmers' costs. It observes that newspapers did not criticize the economic-stabilization directive's demand for increased food production.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 22: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending January 13, 1949
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch analyzes metropolitan and prefectural newspaper comment on labor legislation, policing, elections, the purge and agricultural quotas.
subfiles.summary: Japanese editorials generally treated proposed labor-law amendments as a response to unions' lack of restraint while insisting that collective bargaining and strike rights would remain. Newspapers discussed the Allied Council's examination of Japanese policing, the succession of Dean Acheson to George Marshall, weak election interest, and alleged defects in campaign restrictions. The despatch also describes Yoshida's abortive proposal for a purge-appeal committee and provincial concern over the squeeze between low farm prices and high production costs. It concludes with limited coverage of Arthur Raper's observations on rural Japan.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 39: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending January 20, 1949
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch surveys press discussion immediately before the January 23 election and reactions to foreign-investment policy, the exchange rate and proposals for an Asian defense pact.
subfiles.summary: Newspapers deplored voter apathy, debated party versus candidate loyalty, and criticized the publicly managed campaign system; they also considered the constitutional vote on Supreme Court justices. The despatch reports Communist claims of socialist-communist unity and the Socialist press's rejection of those claims. Editorials cautiously welcomed foreign capital while connecting it to price stabilization and a single yen-dollar rate. Press speculation also focused on Kenneth Royall's impending visit and the possibility of a Far Eastern defense arrangement amid events in China and Indonesia.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 58: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending January 27, 1949
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch analyzes Japanese editorial interpretations of the January 23 House of Representatives election.
subfiles.summary: The press concentrated on the Democratic Liberal landslide, the Communist Party's rise from four to thirty-five seats, and the high voter turnout. Editorialists debated whether the results heralded a dangerous polarization between the conservative right and Communist left, and they blamed the Katayama and Ashida governments for the collapse of centrist parties. Several papers urged the Socialist Party to reform itself. Jiji Shimpo and Yomiuri opposed Democratic participation in a coalition with Yoshida and favored a clear parliamentary opposition and consolidation of ideologically similar parties.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 71: Japanese Newspaper Reactions for the Week Ending February 3, 1949
subfiles.from: W. J. Sebald, United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch reviews press treatment of Stalin's peace proposal, labor-management cooperation, party realignment, purge appeals and Secretary Royall's visit.
subfiles.summary: Two newspapers treated Stalin's peace statement skeptically, with Nihon Keizai arguing that Soviet policy made peace declarations unreliable. Extensive editorials on the Tokyo Labor-Management Conference urged cooperation, increased production, shared burdens and self-help under the Economic Stabilization Program. The press also discussed the Socialist Party's refusal to merge with the Communists and the Yoshida government's proposed Public Officials Re-screening Committee. Secretary Royall's visit prompted speculation about economic stabilization, the yen-dollar rate, China and American strategy in the Far East.

subfiles.title: Tokyo Despatch No. 83: Transmitting Copies of The Japanese Press, Past and Present, 1949
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The despatch transmits five copies of a handbook prepared by the Japan Newspaper Publishers' and Editors' Association.
subfiles.summary: In accordance with standing instructions, the Acting Political Adviser forwards five copies of The Japanese Press, Past and Present, 1949. The publication was prepared and issued by the Japan Newspaper Publishers' and Editors' Association.

subfiles.title: The Japanese Press, Past and Present, 1949
subfiles.from: Japan Newspaper Publishers' and Editors' Association
subfiles.about: The opening of this English-language handbook describes the geography, institutions, ethics, organization and history of the Japanese newspaper industry.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure begins with a map of newspaper publication centers, title pages, a list of association publications, a foreword by Masanori Ito, a detailed contents list and advertisements for Japanese newspapers and advertising services. Its first substantive article recounts the founding, organization, committees, publications, educational work and other activities of the Japan Newspaper Publishers' and Editors' Association. The Canons of Journalism proclaim press freedom, factual reporting, responsible editorial comment, impartiality, tolerance and professional decency. The opening historical chapter traces Japanese newspapers from translations of Dutch material through early Meiji regulation and the emergence of important early papers.
